query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A light thermomechanical processing step—specifically, a controlled cold rolling reduction combined with a subsequent low‐temperature annealing—will refine the lamellar spacing and induce subtle phase adjustment in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy, thereby enhancing yield strength, ductility, resistance to room-temperature creep, and corrosion performance under extreme service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with a uniform, fine lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure showing moderate strength and plasticity.
generation.intervention: Apply a single-step thermomechanical treatment consisting of a modest cold rolling reduction (e.g., approximately 8% thickness reduction) followed by an optimized low-temperature annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: Processing carried out at room temperature (cold rolling) then annealing at a low to moderate temperature (e.g., near 700°C for a short time) to induce partial recrystallization without coarsening; intended for fasteners operating under extreme temperature fluctuations (ambient to ~700°C), long-term mechanical loading conditions including room-temperature creep, and in corrosive environments (e.g., saline or industrial atmospheres).
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar spacing with a more heterogeneous, ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure and improved phase boundary characteristics that act as barriers to dislocation motion and crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: Cold rolling introduces a high dislocation density and refines the eutectic lamellar interfaces. The subsequent anneal partially recrystallizes the deformed structure while preserving a finer lamellar spacing. This refinement increases the work-hardening rate, strengthens the alloy via grain-boundary and interface strengthening, improves creep resistance by impeding dislocation movement, and reduces local compositional heterogeneities that can accelerate corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated state, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield and fracture strengths while retaining or even enhancing ductility, improved room-temperature creep resistance, and better corrosion behavior due to the stabilized nanostructure and optimized phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with moderate industrial performance in strength and plasticity.
generation.boundary: The intervention is targeted for applications such as fasteners where operating conditions include cyclical extreme temperatures (up to about 700°C), continuous mechanical loading (with notable room-temperature creep potential), and corrosive environments. Its effectiveness should be verified within these temperature and environmental ranges without severe degradation of ductility.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum parameters (e.g., exact rolling reduction percentage, annealing temperature and time) may need fine-tuning to balance improvements in strength, creep resistance, and corrosion behavior without overly sacrificing ductility. The long-term thermal stability of the refined microstructure under service conditions also requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy: one with the proposed cold rolling (≈8% reduction) plus low-temperature annealing treatment and one as the untreated control (as-cast). Test both batches under simulated service conditions that include cyclic thermal exposure (room temperature up to ~700°C), sustained mechanical loading to assess creep, and immersion in a corrosive (e.g., 3.5% NaCl) environment.
measurements: Tensile tests to measure yield and fracture strengths and elongation
Creep tests at room temperature under sustained load
Corrosion rate measurements via potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/EBSD) to confirm lamellar refinement and phase stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically processed alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical strength (yield and fracture), creep resistance, and corrosion performance compared to the as-cast state, or if the refined microstructure degrades during thermal cycling, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: These results showed that the yield strength (1437 ± 26 MPa), tensile strength (1562 ± 33 MPa), and elongation (14 ± 1%) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy after annealing at low temperature were significantly improved compared with the as-cast alloy. Eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit an excellent balance of toughness and strength at room temperature. However, there is still an immediate requirement to design structural components with more strength and ductility due to the increasing technical requirements and harsher operating environments in industrial applications. The demand for stronger and more ductile structural elements has increased as airplane components have become more demanding and technical standards have advanced. Therefore, it is of significance to develop a new eutectic high-entropy alloy with superior properties based on AlCoCrFeNi2.1.

The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
